gloss: tomorrow, the morrow, time to come; price, hire
summary: מָחָר is tomorrow, the day after today (Exo 16:23; 1Sa 20:5), and so the time to come, when a son will ask what the Passover or the stones of Jordan mean (Exo 13:14; Jos 4:6). מָחֳרָת is the morrow reckoned from a day already named: the next day in a narrative, and in the law “the morrow after the sabbath”, the day the sheaf of firstfruits is waved and from which fifty days are counted to the feast of weeks (Lev 23:11, 15–16). מְחִיר, price or hire, what is paid for a thing (2Sa 24:24; Isa 55:1), is written with the same consonants, but nothing yet shown ties it to “tomorrow”. The Aramaic of the Targums and the Peshitta keeps מְחַר for tomorrow.

words.summary: A noun used as an adverb: the day after this one, often set beside “today” or fixed by “about this time”; and more loosely any day still to come, as when children ask in later generations.

senses.definition: The day following the present day, counted from today: what is to be done or will happen when this day has passed.

evidence.note: On the sixth day, when twice the manna is gathered: “מָחָר is a שַׁבָּתוֹן, a holy sabbath to Yahweh”; bake today what you will bake.
“Make them holy today and tomorrow”, and be ready for the third day (Exo 19:11).
“Behold, tomorrow is the new moon”; on the morrow of it, the second day, David’s place is empty (1Sa 20:27).
“About this time tomorrow, the third day”.
“We will eat him today, and we will eat my son tomorrow.”
“Stay here today also, and tomorrow I will send you away”; and he stayed that day and the next (מִמָּחֳרָת).
Let it be granted tomorrow also, according to today’s decree.
Pharaoh names the day for the frogs to be taken away: “tomorrow”.
“Tomorrow this sign shall be.”
Yahweh appoints a set time: “Tomorrow Yahweh will do this thing in the land”, and he does it the next day (Exo 9:6).
“About this time tomorrow” the hail.
“Tomorrow I will stand on the top of the hill with the staff of God in my hand.”
Aaron proclaims “a feast to Yahweh tomorrow” before the calf.
“Make yourselves holy for tomorrow, and you shall eat flesh.”
“Make yourselves holy, for tomorrow Yahweh will do wonders among you.”
“If you do not save your life tonight, tomorrow you will be killed.”
“Tomorrow you and your sons will be with me”: Saul and his sons fall on Gilboa the next day (1Sa 31:2–8).
“Eat and drink, for tomorrow we die.”
The drunken watchmen: “tomorrow will be as this day, great beyond measure.”
“Do not say to your neighbour, Go and come again, and tomorrow I will give, when you have it with you”: put off past today.
“Do not boast of יוֹם מָחָר, for you do not know what a day will bring forth.”

senses.definition: A day not counted from today but still to come: the later time when children who did not see the event will ask about it, or when a deed will be judged.

evidence.note: “When your son asks you מָחָר, What is this?” The question of a later generation about the redemption of the firstborn.
“When your son asks you מָחָר, What are the testimonies…?”, answered with the bringing out of Egypt.
“When your children ask מָחָר, What do these stones mean to you?”
The eastern tribes built the altar lest “מָחָר your children say to our children, What have you to do with Yahweh?”
“When they say so to us or to our generations מָחָר”.
“My righteousness will answer for me בְּיוֹם מָחָר, when you come to see my wages”: any later day of reckoning.

evidence.locator: Exo.16.23, מָחָר → αὔριον; Isa.22.13, מָחָר → αὔριον; Pro.27.1, מָחָר → αὔριον; αὔριον renders מָחָר ×44

evidence.note: Quotes Isa 22:13: “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die.”
“Do not be anxious for tomorrow, for tomorrow will be anxious for itself.”
“Today and tomorrow, and the third day I am perfected.”
“You do not know what will be tomorrow”, as Pro 27:1.

opposites.note: Today set against tomorrow: what is done now and what waits a day.

phrases.gloss: the coming day, a day to come
when your son asks you in time to come

words.summary: The day after a day already told, nearly always with מִן (מִמָּחֳרָת, “on the morrow”). Where מָחָר counts forward from today, מָחֳרָת counts from a day the narrative or the law has named: the morrow of the Passover, of the new moon, of the sabbath.

senses.definition: The day following one just narrated or appointed: “on the morrow” after a night, a sacrifice or an event.

evidence.note: After the night just told, “on the morrow” the firstborn speaks of “last night”.
The people gather quail “all that day and all the night and all the next day”: three spans in order.
The peace offering is eaten “on the day you sacrifice it, and on the morrow”; what is left to the third day is burned.
The vowed or freewill offering may be eaten on the day and on the morrow.
Uriah stays in Jerusalem “that day and the next”.
Yahweh had set the time “tomorrow” (Exo 9:5); “on the morrow” he did it.
Aaron proclaimed a feast for tomorrow (Exo 32:5); “they rose early on the morrow” and offered.
On the morrow Aaron’s staff has budded, blossomed and yielded almonds.
“Until the evening of their morrow”, לְמָחֳרָתָם.
The morrow after the battle: Saul fell as was said the night before (1Sa 28:19).
“When the dawn came up on the morrow”.

senses.definition: In the construct, the day after a day the law or the calendar fixes: the morrow of the sabbath, of the Passover, of the new moon, of a day of sacrifice.

evidence.note: The sheaf of the firstfruits: “on the morrow after the sabbath the priest shall wave it”, to be accepted for you.
“You shall count for yourselves from the morrow after the sabbath, from the day you brought the sheaf of the wave offering, seven sabbaths.”
“To the morrow after the seventh sabbath you shall number fifty days”, and offer a new grain offering.
Israel set out from Rameses on the fifteenth day of the first month: “on the morrow of the Passover”, the Passover being the fourteenth (Lev 23:5).
“On the morrow of the Passover” Israel ate of the produce of the land, unleavened cakes and parched grain.
“The manna ceased on the morrow”, after they had eaten of the land’s produce.
“On the morrow of the new moon, the second day”, David’s place is empty again.
Sacrifices “on the morrow after that day”.

greek.gloss: on the morrow, the next day

evidence.locator: Lev.23.11, מָחֳרָת → ἐπαύριον; Lev.23.15, מָחֳרָת → ἐπαύριον; Num.33.3, מָחֳרָת → ἐπαύριον; ἐπαύριον renders מָחֳרָת ×20

evidence.note: “On the morrow, which is after the preparation”: the sabbath, while Christ lay in the tomb.

phrases.gloss: on the morrow after the sabbath
on the morrow of the Passover
they rose early on the morrow

words.gloss: price, hire; what is paid in exchange
words.summary: What is given in exchange for a thing or a service: the price of a field, a vineyard, horses, water and wood, or the hire of a priest who teaches for pay. Often with בְּ, “for a price”, and negated, “for no price”, of what is given or taken without payment. Its tie to the root’s “tomorrow” is not understood; a Sabaean mḫr of sale and Akkadian maḫāru “receive” are the nearest leads, both uncertain.

senses.definition: What is paid to acquire a thing, its value counted in silver or goods.

evidence.note: “I will surely buy it from you בִּמְחִיר; I will not offer burnt offerings to Yahweh my God that cost me nothing”, and he bought it for fifty shekels.
Ahab to Naboth: a better vineyard, or “silver, the מְחִיר of it”.
“The lambs for your clothing, and the goats the מְחִיר of a field.”
“Our water we drink for silver; our wood comes בִּמְחִיר”: in captivity even what was free must be bought.
The king’s merchants took horses from Kue בִּמְחִיר.
Wisdom: “Gold cannot be given for it, nor silver weighed as its מְחִיר.”
“Why is there a מְחִיר in the hand of a fool to buy wisdom, when he has no heart?”
The king of the north “will divide the land בִּמְחִיר”.

senses.gloss: hire, wage, payment for a service
senses.definition: What is paid for a service or a favour, set beside a bribe and a harlot’s hire.

evidence.note: “Her heads judge for a bribe (שֹׁחַד), her priests teach בִּמְחִיר, her prophets divine for silver.”
“The hire (אֶתְנַן) of a harlot or the מְחִיר of a dog” may not be brought into Yahweh’s house for a vow.

senses.definition: Negated (לֹא בִמְחִיר, בְּלוֹא מְחִיר): given, released or lost with nothing paid in return.

evidence.note: “Come, buy and eat; come, buy wine and milk without silver and without מְחִיר.”
Cyrus will build Yahweh’s city and let his exiles go “not for מְחִיר nor for reward (שֹׁחַד)”.
Judah’s wealth given to plunder “not for מְחִיר”.
“You sell your people for no wealth, and have not grown rich by their מְחִיר.”
“You were bought with a price.”
The thirty pieces of silver, “the price of blood”.

evidence.locator: Job.28.15, מְחִיר → ἀντάλλαγμα; ἀντάλλαγμα renders מְחִיר ×3

evidence.note: “What will a man give in exchange for his life?”
“The worker is worthy of his hire.”

parallels.note: A bribe or reward beside a price: payment that buys what should not be sold.
Silver, the means of payment, beside the price paid.
A harlot’s hire beside the price of a dog.

words.summary: The Peshitta’s ܡܚܪ (mḥār), where the Greek has αὔριον, and once for ἐπαύριον: one word for both Hebrew מָחָר and מָחֳרָת.

senses.definition: The day after today, set beside today and the third day; and the day after a named day.

evidence.note: “Do not be anxious for tomorrow, for tomorrow will be anxious for itself.”
“Today and tomorrow, and on the third day I am perfected.”
The grass that is today and tomorrow is cast into the oven.
Isa 22:13 quoted: “for tomorrow we die”.
“You do not know what will be tomorrow; what is your life? A vapour.”
For Greek ἐπαύριον: the day after the preparation.

cognates.note: The Targums’ word for tomorrow: Onkelos at Exo 17:9 and the Targum of Proverbs at 27:1 render Hebrew מָחָר by it, and later Aramaic has מָחְרָא דְּמָחָר “the day after tomorrow”. It answers to both מָחָר and מָחֳרָת, as the Peshitta’s ܡܚܪ does. Aramaic does not keep ḥ and ḫ apart, so it does not show the older sound behind ח.

evidence.locator: M00936, מְחַר (מָחְרָא), Targ. Ex. XVII, 9; Targ. Prov. XXVII, 1

cognates.gloss: sale, deed of sale (sense from context, marked uncertain)
cognates.note: Sabaean nouns mḫr and mḫrtm, “they signed the deeds of gift and sale” (C 435/2), a gift “from the proceeds of the sale” (C 140/8); the dictionary itself compares Hebrew מְחִיר. If it belongs here, it shows ḫ, not ḥ, behind ח in מְחִיר. The sense rests on two contexts and is marked uncertain there, so it is recorded as possible.

evidence.locator: p. 271, MḪR (n. mḫrtm C435/2; mḫr C140/8)

cognates.note: The Akkadian verb of facing and of receiving (a payment, a gift); the noun of price formed from it would give what is received in exchange, the sense of מְחִיר. The derived noun has not yet been followed to its dictionary page, so the link stays possible. Akkadian maḫru “front; (of time) the past” is the same verb’s noun and points backward in time, not forward, so it is no evidence for מָחָר “tomorrow”.

doctrine.statement: The sheaf of the first of the harvest is brought to the priest and waved before Yahweh “on the morrow after the sabbath”, to be accepted for Israel, and no bread or parched grain of the new harvest may be eaten until that day (Lev 23:10–14); from that morrow seven sabbaths are counted, fifty days, to the new grain offering of the feast of weeks (Lev 23:15–16). Christ was laid in the tomb on the preparation, the women rested on the sabbath, and the next day, the morrow after the preparation, was that sabbath (Luk 23:54–56; Mat 27:62); he was raised early on the first day of the week, the day after the sabbath (Mat 28:1; Mrk 16:9). Paul calls him “the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep”, Christ the firstfruits and afterward those who are Christ’s at his coming (1Co 15:20, 23), and on the day of Pentecost, the fiftieth day, the spirit was poured out (Act 2:1–4). From the verses: the morrow after the sabbath, the day the first sheaf of the harvest was presented to be accepted, is the day Christ was raised, the first of the harvest of the dead, and the fifty days counted from it end at the outpouring of the spirit.

When Yahweh called Jerusalem to weeping and sackcloth, it answered with feasting: “Eat and drink, for tomorrow we die”, and Yahweh swore that iniquity would not be covered till they died (Isa 22:12–14). Paul takes up their words: if the dead are not raised, those who have fallen asleep in Christ have perished, and “let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die” (1Co 15:18, 32). From the verses: Paul allows no hope after death but resurrection. If the dead are not raised, death ends the man, and the revellers’ reasoning would stand; because Christ is raised, the morrow on which a man dies is not his end.

“Do not boast of tomorrow, for you do not know what a day will bring forth” (Pro 27:1); the watchmen who say “tomorrow will be as this day” are blind dogs (Isa 56:10–12). James sets the same words against those who plan a year’s trade: “you do not know what will be tomorrow… you ought to say, If the Lord wills, we shall live and do this or that” (Jas 4:13–15), and Jesus tells his disciples not to be anxious for tomorrow but to seek first the kingdom of God (Mat 6:33–34). From the verses: tomorrow is in God’s hand, not man’s, so a man plans under God’s will and does not put off the good he can do today (Pro 3:28).

Yahweh calls the thirsty to come and buy wine and milk “without silver and without מְחִיר”, and to hear, that their soul may live (Isa 55:1–3); his exiles are let go “not for price nor reward” (Isa 45:13). Against this, Jerusalem’s priests teach for a price (Mic 3:11). The invitation is taken up at the end: “let whoever is thirsty come; whoever will, let him take the water of life freely” (Rev 22:17; 21:6), and Jesus sends out the twelve with “freely you received, freely give” (Mat 10:8). Yet David would not offer to Yahweh what cost him nothing (2Sa 24:24), and the believer is “bought with a price” (1Co 6:20). From the verses: what Yahweh gives, life and deliverance, cannot be bought and is given without price; the price was paid, not by the one who receives it, and what is offered back to God is not to be had for nothing.

note: Root key מחר as the corpus keys it. Words: מָחָר (m.bq.ab), מָחֳרָת (m.bq.ac), מְחִיר (m.bq.ad). BDB’s m.bq.ae, the name Mehir (1Ch 4:11), is left for a name entry not written here (not one of this task’s names); its tokens overlap m.bq.ad in the database (1Ki 21:2, Isa 55:1, Pro 17:16, 1Ch 4:11 counted under both), so 1Ch 4:11 is counted under the price word until the name is written. m.bq.ao (מַטְאֲטֵא, broom, Isa 14:23) belongs to טאטא and is left out. The derivation of מָחָר is not settled: some take it as a prefixed form of אחר “be behind” (*maʾḥar, “the later day”), which would make it another root’s word; others as Akkadian maḫru “front”, which in time means the former, not the coming, day. Neither is cited. No Arabic cognate found: Lane’s محر and مخر (a ship cleaving water) are unrelated. Ugaritic “tomorrow” in the letter 3.5:15 (Segert’s glossary) is šḥr, not mḥr. Krahmalkov has no Phoenician mḥr “tomorrow”. Leads not followed: Imperial Aramaic (l)mḥr “tomorrow” (Segert cites it; check CAL); CAD M/1 s.v. maḫīru “price, exchange rate” for מְחִיר (page not checked; Oracc lacks the noun). Doctrine on the morrow after the sabbath: Lev 23 does not name which sabbath; the doctrine rests on the first day of the week of the resurrection, not on settling that question; Jos 5:11 (new grain eaten on the morrow of the Passover) bears on it.
